content: 1. Magnesium sulfate and potassium chloride can increase the toxicity of amikacin liposome inhalation. This interaction may occur due to the potential for these agents to cause fluid and electrolyte abnormalities, which can elevate the risk of adverse events such as seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is recommended when these agents are co-administered. 2. Sodium sulfate, potassium sulfate, and magnesium sulfate can also increase the toxicity of amikacin liposome inhalation. Similar to the above, this interaction is likely due to fluid and electrolyte imbalances, which can heighten the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal dysfunction. Use caution and monitor patients closely. 3. The combination of voclosporin and amikacin liposome inhalation may increase the toxicity of either drug through mechanisms involving nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Therapy should be modified as needed, and patients should be closely monitored. Co-administration with drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may elevate the risk of both acute and chronic kidney damage. 4. Co-administration of amikacin liposome inhalation and entecavir may increase the effects of either drug by reducing renal clearance. While the clinical significance of this interaction is uncertain, it is important to note that drugs that impair renal function or compete for active tubular secretion may raise serum concentrations of either entecavir or the co-administered drug. 5. Amikacin liposome inhalation has been associated with an increased risk of respiratory adverse reactions, including hypersensitivity pneumonitis, hemoptysis, bronchospasm, and exacerbation of underlying pulmonary diseases. These events have led to hospitalizations in some cases. If hypersensitivity pneumonitis occurs, the drug should be discontinued, and appropriate medical management should be initiated. 6. Hemoptysis has been reported with amikacin liposome inhalation. If this occurs, it should be managed as clinically appropriate. 7. Bronchospasm, including symptoms such as asthma, bronchial hyperreactivity, dyspnea, and wheezing, has been reported. If bronchospasm occurs, it should be treated as medically necessary. 8. Exacerbations of underlying pulmonary diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or bronchiectasis, have been observed in clinical trials. If exacerbations occur, they should be managed appropriately. 9. Nephrotoxicity has been observed in patients with Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease during clinical trials. Aminoglycosides, including amikacin, are known to be associated with nephrotoxicity. Patients with known or suspected renal dysfunction should be closely monitored. 10. Patients with neuromuscular disorders, such as myasthenia gravis, were not included in clinical trials. Aminoglycosides may exacerbate muscle weakness by inhibiting acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions. Patients with known or suspected neuromuscular disorders should be monitored closely. 11. Amikacin liposome inhalation may cause fetal harm if administered to a pregnant woman. Although systemic absorption following inhalation is expected to be low, aminoglycosides, including inhaled amikacin, have been associated with irreversible bilateral congenital deafness when administered during pregnancy. Pregnant women should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. 12. There is no data on the presence of inhaled amikacin in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or its impact on milk production. However, limited data from other routes of administration suggest that amikacin is present in human milk. Systemic absorption following inhalation is expected to be low. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. 13. Systemically absorbed amikacin is primarily eliminated via glomerular filtration. Unabsorbed amikacin following inhalation is likely eliminated through cellular turnover and expectoration. 14. Before use, the suspension should be at room temperature. Shake the vial well for at least 10–15 seconds until the contents appear uniform and well-mixed. Pour the suspension into the medication reservoir of the nebulizer handset. This medication is for oral inhalation use only and should be administered using the Lamira Nebulizer System. 15. If the patient also uses a bronchodilator, they should use the bronchodilator first, following its instructions, before using amikacin liposome inhalation. Consider pretreatment with short-acting selective beta-2 agonists for patients with known hyperreactive airway disease, COPD, asthma, or bronchospasm. 16. If a dose is missed, the next dose should be administered the following day. Patients should not double the dose to make up for the missed dose. 17. The medication should be refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F) until the expiration date on the vial. Do not freeze. It may be stored at room temperature (up to 25°C [77°F]) for up to 4 weeks. Once stored at room temperature, any unused drug should be discarded at the end of 4 weeks.
